categories.name: Fermented & Funky
categories.blurb: Time is the secret ingredient. Kimchi, doenjang, and the slow-built funk that starts it all.

categories.name: Charred & Smoky
categories.blurb: Fire meets flesh. Grilled, broiled, and blistered until the edges go black and sweet.

categories.name: Noodles & Broth
categories.blurb: Slurp-worthy strands and deep, layered bowls. Chewy, saucy, or swimming in broth.

categories.name: Rice & Bowls
categories.blurb: One bowl, everything in it. Crisp-bottomed rice built for mixing hard at the table.

categories.name: Small Plates & Banchan
categories.blurb: Snacks with swagger. Street food, banchan, and the plates you fight over.

categories.name: Braises & Stews

categories.name: Sweet Heat

dishes.name: Gochujang-Glazed Galbi Short Ribs
dishes.shortDesc: Thick English-cut short ribs, braised low in a gochujang-soy bath until the connective tissue surrenders, then glazed hard under the broiler: this is the record where the paste does all…
dishes.longDesc: Thick English-cut short ribs, braised low in a gochujang-soy bath until the connective tissue surrenders, then glazed hard under the broiler: this is the record where the paste does all four of its jobs at once — it seasons the braise, sweetens the glaze, carries the ferment's depth through three hours of heat, and lacquers at the end.
ingredients: 1.8 kg English-cut bone-in beef short ribs (thick, 5–7 cm blocks)
1 tbsp neutral oil (about 12 g)
1 large onion (about 200 g), thick-sliced; 6 cloves garlic (about 24 g), smashed; a 5 cm piece of ginger (about 25 g), sliced
4 tbsp gochujang (about 80 g)
60 ml soy sauce
2 tbsp honey (about 40 g)
1 tbsp mirin (15 ml)
1 Asian pear (about 300 g), quartered (the braise's tenderizer and body — strained out later)
700 ml water or beef stock
2 dried chilies or 1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g), for dial 3
The braising liquid, reduced
1 tbsp honey (about 20 g), extra
A squeeze of lemon or splash of rice vinegar (about 10 ml)
Steamed rice (about 600 g cooked), scallion threads, sesame seeds (about 8 g), quick-pickled radish or cucumber
method: The braise: seared ribs, aromatics, and everything liquid into the pot. The gochujang fried in the fond for 30 seconds before the liquids join (the bloom — the spine's first law), then soy, honey, mirin, pear, water, and the chilies over the ribs. Lid ajar, the barest simmer (a bubble every few seconds — 95 °C at the pot's edge, never a boil), 2.5–3 hours, turning the ribs once at the halfway mark.

Strain and reduce — the glaze is the braise, concentrated. Ribs out to a tray; the liquid through a fine strainer (the pear and aromatics have given everything — discard them), the fat spooned off the top, and the remaining liquid reduced at a hard simmer, 15–25 minutes, to a sauce that coats a spoon and holds a dragged trail. Taste: it should be intense — salty-sweet-fermented, a shade too strong alone — and then the extra honey and the lemon go in to round it.

The broiler lacquer. Ribs on a foil-lined tray, glaze brushed thick on all meat faces, and under a hot broiler (or a 230 °C oven's top rack) 3–4 minutes a side, watching through the door — the sugars go from lacquered to burnt in one careless minute. Two coats, two broiler passes, for the full build.
Serve on rice with the remaining glaze at the table — there should be a small bowl of it, because the ribs' last act is dragging rice through the leftover lacquer.

dishes.name: Baechu Kimchi
dishes.shortDesc: Straight talk, because this site runs on it: traditional kimchi does not use gochujang. The pot's chile arrives as gochugaru flakes, and any jar telling you otherwise is selling shortcuts.
dishes.longDesc: Straight talk, because this site runs on it: traditional kimchi does not use gochujang.
ingredients: 1 large head napa cabbage (about 1.5 kg), cut into bite squares (the fast build cuts small — more surface, faster ferment)
1/2 cup coarse salt (about 100 g), dissolved in water to cover
1/2 cup gochugaru (about 50 g)
1.5 tbsp gochujang (about 30 g) — the modern marker
3 tbsp fish sauce (about 45 ml)
1 tbsp salted shrimp or extra fish sauce (about 15 g)
8 cloves garlic (about 32 g), grated; a thumb of ginger (about 20 g), grated
1/2 Asian pear (about 100 g), grated
1 tsp sugar (about 4 g)
100 g Korean radish, fine matchsticks; 4 scallions (about 60 g), cut
method: The paste whisked into a thick slurry — gochugaru, gochujang, fish sauce, shrimp, garlic, ginger, pear, sugar — then the radish and scallions folded through.

The squeezed cabbage and paste massaged together by hand (gloves save your weekend) until every square wears the coat, packed into a clean jar — pressed hard, 3 cm of headspace, weight on top, loose lid.
The faster clock: room temperature 2–4 days at normal kitchen warmth (the traditional batch's window assumes a cooler kitchen), tasting from day two.

dishes.name: Rosé Tteokbokki
dishes.shortDesc: Rosé tteokbokki is the modern café era's great invention: the street cart's fiery rice-cake stew mellowed with cream into a blush-pink, tomato-sweet sauce that keeps the paste's ferment…
dishes.longDesc: Rosé tteokbokki is the modern café era's great invention: the street cart's fiery rice-cake stew mellowed with cream into a blush-pink, tomato-sweet sauce that keeps the paste's ferment under the dairy's calm.
ingredients: 400 g cylinder rice cakes (tteokbokki tteok), soaked 20 minutes in cold water if shelf-stable, rinsed if refrigerated-fresh
1 tbsp butter (about 15 g)
2 cloves garlic (about 8 g), sliced
3 tbsp gochujang (about 60 g)
2 tbsp tomato paste or ketchup (about 30 g)
1 tbsp honey (about 20 g)
1 tbsp soy sauce (15 ml)
250 ml water or anchovy-kelp stock
80 ml heavy cream
1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g), for dial 2-and-a-half
100 g fish cake sheets, torn; 2 scallions (about 30 g), cut into batons; 1/2 onion (about 75 g), sliced; optional: 3 boiled eggs, parboiled cabbage, instant-noodle block for the last 3 minutes
Black pepper; a handful of shredded mozzarella (about 50 g), for the molten fork; Parmesan (about 15 g), the boldest fork of all
method: The bloomed paste pot: butter, garlic, gochujang, tomato paste, honey, and soy fried to a dark rust; the water in, stirred smooth, and brought to a simmer.
Rice cakes, fish cake, and onion into the simmering sauce, 8–10 minutes at a steady bubble, stirring often — the rice cakes soften and the sauce thickens as their surface starch joins it.

The cream, at the end and gently: the pot off its hard boil, the cream poured in a stream while stirring, back to the barest bubble 2 minutes — never a hard boil again, or the cream's proteins tighten and the sauce splits grainy.
The cheese forks: mozzarella melted over for the pull, parmesan grated over for the boldest café register — or neither, the purist's rosé.

dishes.name: Dolsot Bibimbap
dishes.shortDesc: Dolsot bibimbap is the stone bowl's rice feast: the bowl seared screaming hot so the rice at the bottom fries to a golden crust while the arranged vegetables, meat, and egg sit steaming…
dishes.longDesc: Dolsot bibimbap is the stone bowl's rice feast: the bowl seared screaming hot so the rice at the bottom fries to a golden crust while the arranged vegetables, meat, and egg sit steaming above, everything mixed at the table with a spoon of gochujang.
ingredients: 400 g short-grain rice, cooked slightly firm, kept hot
100 g spinach, blanched, squeezed, cut — dressed with 1 tsp sesame oil and salt
100 g bean sprouts, blanched 3 minutes — sesame oil, salt, garlic whisper
100 g carrots, fine-julienned — stir-fried 2 minutes, salt, sesame
100 g zucchini or mushrooms, sliced — stir-fried 2 minutes, salt, sesame
100 g spinach's winter cousin or gosari (#B16's lane) if found
200 g ground beef or thinly sliced brisket — stir-fried with 1 tbsp soy, 1 tsp honey, garlic, sesame oil
4 eggs (about 200 g), fried sunny-side or left raw-yolked for the stone bowl's heat

4 tbsp gochujang (about 80 g), 2 tbsp honey or syrup (about 40 g), 1 tbsp sesame oil (15 ml), 1 tbsp water (15 ml), 2 cloves garlic (about 8 g) grated, 1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g) — stirred to a spooning sauce; gochugaru (about 3 g) on the side for dial-raisers
4 stone bowls (dolsot) or a cast-iron skillet per two diners — the honest bridge
method: The assembly, per bowl: a film of sesame oil (about 4 ml) swirled in the screaming-hot bowl, then hot rice pressed into the bowl's floor and up its walls — the rice touching the stone fries while the toppings go on top, arranged in wedges: each vegetable in its own sector, the meat at the center, the egg crowning.
The wait — 3–4 minutes over the flame still, or 2 on the trivet — while the crust builds at the bowl's floor.
At the table: a spoon of sauce over, then the mix — the diner stirs their own bowl violently, egg and sauce and sectors and crust fragments folded through the rice into one speckled whole.

dishes.name: Doenjang Jjigae
dishes.shortDesc: Straight talk: doenjang jjigae uses no gochujang at all.
dishes.longDesc: Straight talk: doenjang jjigae uses no gochujang at all.
ingredients: 800 ml water; a 10 cm piece of dried kelp (about 5 g), 6–8 dried anchovies (about 10 g), simmered 10 minutes and strained — or water, honestly, and a longer simmer
3 tbsp doenjang (about 60 g)
1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g) — the pot's only chile, and a modest one
1 tsp gochujang (about 5 g), optional — the modern kitchen's bridge, and the reason this pot is here; the traditional pot skips it
150 g firm tofu, cubed; 100 g zucchini, half-moons; 100 g potato or onion, sliced; 100 g kimchi (#2's jar), chopped if sour-aged
2 scallions (about 30 g) and 2 green chilies (about 15 g), sliced; 3 cloves garlic (about 12 g), grated; a splash of sesame oil to finish (about 5 ml)
A handful of enoki or shiitake mushrooms (about 60 g), optional
method: The dissolved paste, the gochugaru, and the optional gochujang into the simmering stock; the potato, onion, and zucchini in; 8 minutes at a steady bubble — the root vegetables need the head start.
The tofu, kimchi, and mushrooms in, 5 more minutes — the tofu warms through and the kimchi's sour edge dissolves into the broth's depth.
Garlic, scallions, chilies, and the sesame oil finish over the top, pot off the heat, straight to the table in its own vessel.

dishes.name: Yangnyeom Fried Chicken
dishes.shortDesc: Korean fried chicken's argument with the American original is thinness of crust and the sauce: a shattering, thin glass crust from a double fry, and — in the yangnyeom register — a…
dishes.longDesc: Korean fried chicken's argument with the American original is thinness of crust and the sauce: a shattering, thin glass crust from a double fry, and — in the yangnyeom register — a gochujang glaze tossed at the last second, lacquering every crevice without ever sogging the crunch.
ingredients: 1.2 kg chicken wings and drumettes (or boneless thighs cut into strips)

500 ml water, 2 tbsp salt (about 30 g), 2 tbsp sugar (about 25 g), 4 cloves garlic (about 16 g) smashed, a thumb of ginger (about 10 g) sliced — dissolved, then the chicken in, refrigerated 2 hours (up to 4)
120 g potato starch or cornstarch
40 g all-purpose flour
1/2 tsp each salt and pepper (about 4 g)
A pinch of baking powder (about 2 g)
About 1.5 liters neutral oil, for the two-stage fry
2 tbsp gochujang (about 40 g)
2 tbsp honey or corn syrup (about 40 g)
1 tbsp soy sauce (15 ml)
1 tbsp mirin (15 ml)
1 tsp gochugaru (about 3 g) — dial control
1 tbsp neutral oil (about 12 g); 3 cloves garlic (about 12 g), grated; 1 tsp toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g)
Optional: 1/2 tbsp ketchup (about 10 g), the old-school register
method: First fry — cook through: oil at 170 °C (a starch-dusted cube sizzles steadily, not violently), the chicken in uncrowded batches, 6–8 minutes to cooked-through and pale-gold. Drain on a rack.
Second fry — the shatter: oil up to 190 °C, the same pieces returned for 90 seconds to 2 minutes, until the crust goes deep gold and audibly crackles when two pieces touch.

The fifteen-second toss — the sauce's law. The hot chicken into the wide bowl, the warm glaze over, and tossed with two spatulas for ten to fifteen seconds — every surface lacquered, the bowl scraped, service immediate.

dishes.name: Buldak Fire Noodles
dishes.shortDesc: Buldak — "fire chicken" — is the Korean fire-noodle phenomenon's parent dish: chicken tossed in a sauce that runs the scale's ceiling, over chewy noodles, with the cheese-and-rice relief…
dishes.longDesc: Buldak — "fire chicken" — is the Korean fire-noodle phenomenon's parent dish: chicken tossed in a sauce that runs the scale's ceiling, over chewy noodles, with the cheese-and-rice relief protocol built into the service.
ingredients: 500 g chicken thigh, bite-cubed
1 tbsp neutral oil (about 12 g)
3 tbsp gochujang (about 60 g)
2 tbsp gochugaru (about 12 g) — the main heat engine; 1 tbsp for dial 3
1 tbsp soy sauce (15 ml); 1 tbsp honey (about 20 g); 1 tbsp mirin (15 ml)
2 cloves garlic (about 8 g) and a thumb of ginger (about 10 g), grated
1 tsp curry powder or gochujang's street-cart companion (about 3 g) — the buldak carts' signature note
1 tbsp neutral oil, for frying the sauce
60 ml water or stock
300 g thick chewy wheat noodles (udon, knife-cut, or the instant blocks, sauce discarded)
The lawful coolants: shredded mozzarella (about 60 g), a fried egg or two, cold rice (about 200 g cooked), cucumber sticks, milk in the fridge
method: The chicken seared hard in the oil, 4–5 minutes to browned edges (the sauce will coat; the char stays).

The sauce fried onto the chicken — the pan's heat dropped to medium, the sauce and the 60 ml of water in, stirred and fried 3–4 minutes until it darkens, thickens, and coats every piece in a glossy lacquer.
The noodles boiled to the chewy side of their clock, drained, and tossed through the fire sauce in the pan — 60 seconds, every strand lacquered.

The service: the cheese melted over the top (the dairy carrier law, taming as it melts), the fried egg crowning, cucumber and cold rice armed — the rice-in-the-sauce finish is the traditional last course, the sauce's leftovers seasoned onto the starch.

dishes.name: Gochujang Bolognese
dishes.shortDesc: The fusion test at its strictest: gochujang in a ragù must deepen what the soffritto, the tomato, and the milk were already doing — not turn the plate spicy-red and Korean.
dishes.longDesc: The fusion test at its strictest: gochujang in a ragù must deepen what the soffritto, the tomato, and the milk were already doing — not turn the plate spicy-red and Korean.
ingredients: 2 tbsp olive oil (about 25 g); 100 g pancetta or thick bacon, diced
1 onion (about 150 g), 1 carrot (about 100 g), 1 celery stalk (about 80 g) — pulsed to a fine soffritto in the processor
500 g ground beef (or half beef, half pork)
2 tbsp tomato paste (about 30 g); 2 tbsp gochujang (about 40 g)
250 ml dry white wine (or the honest swap: 200 ml water plus a tablespoon of vinegar)
800 g canned whole tomatoes, crushed by hand
150 ml whole milk
1 bay leaf; salt (about 5 g) and pepper
30 g parmesan rind, if the cheese drawer offers one — the braise's umami ally
400 g tagliatelle or spaghetti
40 g parmesan, grated, plus more at the table; a knob of butter (about 15 g), for the finish
method: The pancetta rendered in the oil until its fat runs and its edges crisp; the soffritto in and softened slowly, 8–10 minutes to sweet and gold — no browning, the Italian law intact.

The bloom, at the doctrine's hinge: the tomato paste and the gochujang into the soffritto's fat together, fried and stirred 60–90 seconds until both darken and the pan smells of tomato-caramel with a warm, savory hum beneath it.

The ground beef in and broken to a crumble, browned through the paste coating; the wine to scrape the fond, simmering off its raw edge 2 minutes; the tomatoes, the rind, the bay, and salt; then the barest simmer, lid ajar, 1.5–2 hours, stirring each half hour — and the milk stirred in at the last 30 minutes, the traditional finish that rounds the acid.
The pasta pulled a minute shy and finished in the ragù with a ladle of its water; the butter and parmesan through the toss.

dishes.name: Kimchi Jjigae
dishes.shortDesc: Kimchi jjigae is the pot the kimchi jar (#2) was always becoming: sour, elder-stage kimchi stewed with pork and tofu and a paste-and-gochugaru broth until the whole pot tastes of the…
dishes.longDesc: Kimchi jjigae is the pot the kimchi jar (#2) was always becoming: sour, elder-stage kimchi stewed with pork and tofu and a paste-and-gochugaru broth until the whole pot tastes of the ferment's second life.
ingredients: 400 g sour, well-fermented baechu kimchi (#2's elder stage or any jar two-plus weeks old), cut into bite lengths, juice included
200 g pork belly or shoulder, sliced 5 mm (or a can of tuna in oil — the bachelor classic, honestly labeled)
400 ml water or anchovy-kelp stock
1.5 tbsp gochujang (about 30 g), dissolved
1 tbsp gochugaru (about 6 g)
1 tbsp soy sauce or the kimchi jar's brine (15 ml)
A pinch of sugar (about 3 g) — rounding, not sweetening

200 g firm tofu, thick-slabbed; 1 onion (about 100 g), sliced; 2 scallions (about 30 g) and 1 green chili (about 8 g), sliced; 3 cloves garlic (about 12 g), grated; 5 ml sesame oil, finishing; instant ramen noodles or cooked rice for the pot's final act, optional
method: The pork rendered in the dry pot first — 3–4 minutes, its fat becoming the pot's cooking base (the tuna path: the oil and the drained fish, 2 minutes). The kimchi in over the rendered pork and fried 2 minutes in the fat — this brief fry drives the kimchi's raw sour edge off and deepens the whole pot before any liquid joins.

The stock, the dissolved gochujang, the gochugaru, and the soy in; the onion too. A steady bubble, 10 minutes, lid ajar — the broth turns the kimchi's red-orange and the pork's fat beads at the surface.

The tofu slabs laid in gently, 5 more minutes — warmed through, not boiled apart. The scallions, chili, garlic, and sesame oil over the top, and the pot goes to the table in its own vessel, still bubbling.

dishes.name: Gochujang Birria Tacos
dishes.shortDesc: Birria is Jalisco's chile-braised beef and its dip-fried taco; this build runs the braise's spine with the paste in the flavor stack — gochujang beside the dried chiles, soy beside the…
dishes.longDesc: Birria is Jalisco's chile-braised beef and its dip-fried taco; this build runs the braise's spine with the paste in the flavor stack — gochujang beside the dried chiles, soy beside the salt, the result a consommé that tastes like birria went to Seoul and came back with opinions.
ingredients: 4 guajillo, 2 ancho, and 1 pasilla chile (about 45 g total), stemmed, seeded, torn flat
Boiling water to cover, soaked 30 minutes (or overnight for a smoother blend)
1.5 kg beef chuck or short rib, cut into 5 cm chunks
Salt (about 8 g) and black pepper
1 tbsp neutral oil (about 12 g)
1 onion (about 150 g), quartered; 6 cloves garlic (about 24 g); a 5 cm piece of ginger (about 20 g)
2 tbsp gochujang (about 40 g)
1 tbsp tomato paste (about 15 g)
2 tsp ground cumin (about 5 g); 1 tsp dried Mexican oregano (about 2 g); 4 whole cloves; 1 cinnamon stick
60 ml soy sauce; 1 tbsp apple cider vinegar (15 ml)
1 can crushed tomatoes (400 g); 800 ml beef stock or water
12 corn tortillas
200 g Oaxaca, mozzarella, or queso asadero, shredded
Onion (about 100 g, diced), cilantro (about 15 g), lime (2 wedges per person)
method: Sear the salted beef hard in the oil, all faces, 8–10 minutes — the fond is the braise's floor (#1's law, unchanged across cuisines). The beef out, a splash of the blend scraped into the fond, the whole purée in and fried 3–4 minutes until it darkens and the oil separates at its edges — the chile paste's own bloom stage, the moment the sauce becomes birria.
The crushed tomatoes, the stock, and the remaining chile soak in; the beef back; the barest simmer, lid ajar, 2.5–3 hours, until the beef forks apart.

The two products: the beef lifted and shredded (fat and gristle out), a ladle of skimmed braising liquid stirred back into the meat; the remaining liquid strained and simmered 10 minutes to the dipping consommé — seasoned up with salt, a squeeze of lime, and dial-raising gochugaru or minced fresh chili to taste.

The dip-fried taco: a comal or dry skillet hot (a tortilla dropped on it should puff faintly within 5 seconds — a surface around 200 °C); a tortilla dragged briefly through the consommé's fat layer (the surface gloss, not the deep broth), then laid on the comal 20 seconds, flipped, filled with beef and cheese, folded, and pressed 45 seconds a side until the tortilla crisps at the fold with cheese running at the edges.
The service: three tacos a person, the consommé in cups beside for dipping, onion, cilantro, and lime over everything.

dishes.name: Gochujang-Miso Black Cod
dishes.shortDesc: The famous miso-marinated black cod, rebuilt with the paste in the cure: white miso for its sweetness, gochujang for its heat and depth, a short 24-hour cure where the grill-site's…
dishes.longDesc: The famous miso-marinated black cod, rebuilt with the paste in the cure: white miso for its sweetness, gochujang for its heat and depth, a short 24-hour cure where the grill-site's version (#SF11's doenjang build) runs 48 with a different register.
ingredients: 4 black cod (sablefish) fillets (about 700 g), pin bones pulled
3 tbsp white miso (about 60 g)
2 tbsp gochujang (about 40 g)
2 tbsp mirin (30 ml)
1 tbsp honey (about 20 g)
1 tbsp toasted sesame oil (15 ml)
Neutral oil for the pan (about 10 ml)
Toasted sesame seeds (about 4 g), sliced scallion (about 10 g)
Pickled cucumber or perilla, rice (about 400 g cooked)
method: A heavy pan at medium with the film of oil; fillets in presentation-side-down, 4 minutes to deep tea-brown caramel — the sugars' clock, watched, not set-and-forgotten.

Flip, 3 minutes more on the second side (a fillet's thickness giving 7 minutes total on the pan), and pull at the flake stage — the flesh parts along the grain at a fork's weight, translucent-glossy at the very center.
Sesame and scallion over, plated on rice with the sharp pickle beside.

dishes.name: Gochujang Shakshuka
dishes.shortDesc: Shakshuka's tomato-pepper base runs on sweet fruit, sharp vinegar-edge, warm spice, and richness from eggs and oil — and the paste's ferment-sweet-heat slots into that axis like the…
dishes.longDesc: Shakshuka's tomato-pepper base runs on sweet fruit, sharp vinegar-edge, warm spice, and richness from eggs and oil — and the paste's ferment-sweet-heat slots into that axis like the tradition's own harissa's cousin.
ingredients: 2 tbsp olive oil (about 25 g)
1 onion (about 150 g), sliced; 2 bell peppers, red (about 250 g), sliced
4 cloves garlic (about 16 g), sliced
2 tbsp gochujang (about 40 g)
1 tsp gochugaru or hot paprika (about 3 g); 1 tsp ground cumin (about 2.5 g); a pinch of allspice (about 1 g)
800 g canned crushed tomatoes
1 tbsp soy sauce (15 ml) — the umami bridge, standing where salt would
1 tsp honey or sugar (about 5 g), if the tomatoes run tart
5 eggs (about 250 g)
100 g feta, crumbled; a handful of cilantro or parsley (about 10 g); pickled onion or a squeeze of lemon
Bread (about 300 g), warm, for the sopping
method: Onion and peppers in the oil at medium-high, 8–10 minutes to soft and slumped; the garlic and the paste in, fried together 45 seconds until darkened and fragrant; the gochugaru, cumin, and allspice a 30-second toast in the same pan.

The crushed tomatoes and soy in; a steady simmer 10 minutes, until the sauce thickens enough to hold a spoon's trail and the oil separates in red-orange drops at the edges — the shakshuka doneness sign, unchanged by the substitution.
Five wells in the sauce, an egg into each, lid on, 4–6 minutes to set whites and molten yolks — the egg-window every cuisine respects.
The pan to the table on its trivet, bread armed.

dishes.name: Ssam with Ssamjang
dishes.shortDesc: The ssam table's grammar (the leaf, the sauce, the meat, the fold) belongs to the grill site's tradition (#F01 there); this record is the modern spread — a gochujang-spiked ssamjang,…
dishes.longDesc: The ssam table's grammar (the leaf, the sauce, the meat, the fold) belongs to the grill site's tradition (#F01 there); this record is the modern spread — a gochujang-spiked ssamjang, quick seared fillings, and a build-your-own board that turns a weeknight into a ssam bar.
ingredients: 3 tbsp doenjang (about 60 g)
1.5 tbsp gochujang (about 30 g)
1 tbsp honey (about 20 g)
1 tbsp toasted sesame oil (15 ml)
2 cloves garlic (about 8 g), grated; half a small onion (about 40 g), grated
1 tsp sesame seeds (about 4 g)
2 tbsp gochujang (about 40 g)
1.5 tbsp rice vinegar (about 22 ml)
1 tbsp honey (about 20 g)
A splash of water (about 15 ml) and a pinch of gochugaru (about 1 g)
500 g pork shoulder or belly, sliced 5 mm, seared hot in a lightly oiled pan 2 minutes a side (or the weeknight shortcut: 300 g of good ham or tofu pressed and seared)
Steamed rice (about 500 g cooked), garlic coins (about 30 g), sliced chili (about 10 g)
Lettuce cups and perilla (about 30 leaves), washed and bone-dry
method: The pork seared in batches at high heat, pulled to the board, and scissored into bite pieces.
The board: sauces at center, pork warm beside, leaves, rice, garlic, and chili in their quadrants.
The build, the tradition's own sequence: leaf, a swipe of ssamjang (or the cho-gochujang for the sweet-heat fork), a piece of hot pork, a garlic coin, a pinch of rice, fold, one bite.

dishes.name: Gochujang Dark Chocolate Tart
dishes.shortDesc: Mexican chocolate has known chile for five centuries; this tart is the Korean pantry's entry into that old pairing — a dark chocolate ganache, warm with gochujang's ferment-sweet-heat,…
dishes.longDesc: Mexican chocolate has known chile for five centuries; this tart is the Korean pantry's entry into that old pairing — a dark chocolate ganache, warm with gochujang's ferment-sweet-heat, in a cocoa-shortbread shell, with the salted sesame finish the tradition brings to its own sweets.
ingredients: 150 g all-purpose flour; 30 g cocoa powder; 40 g sugar; a pinch of salt (about 2 g)
90 g cold butter, cubed; 1 egg yolk (about 20 g); 1–2 tbsp ice water
250 g dark chocolate (64–70%), chopped
200 ml heavy cream
1.5 tbsp gochujang (about 30 g) — the full dose; a level tablespoon for dial 1.5
2 tbsp honey (about 40 g)
30 g butter, soft
A pinch of fine salt (about 2 g)
1 tbsp black or toasted sesame seeds (about 8 g), flaky sea salt (about 3 g), and optional: a dusting of gochugaru (about 1 g) across the top, for the last visual tell
method: The cream warmed to a bare simmer with the gochujang and the honey, whisked as it warms until the paste fully dissolves and the cream turns a uniform pale-rose tan.

The ganache built in three additions: the chopped chocolate in a bowl, the hot gochujang cream poured over and waited on 60 seconds, then stirred from the center outward in slow circles — the emulsion building gradually, the gloss arriving in stages, never whisked to froth. The soft butter and salt stirred in at the gloss.
Poured into the cooled shell, the surface smoothed with a spatula's single pass (more passes leave streaks), and chilled 2 hours to a set that trembles slightly at the pan's tap.

The finish and the first slice: sesame seeds and flaky salt scattered over the whole surface, the optional gochugaru's faint red dust across one quadrant (the last visual tell — and the table's game of spotting which slices came from the spicy corner).

stories.title: The Slow Fire: Why Gochujang Takes a Year
stories.excerpt: Real gochujang isn't cooked—it's grown. We trace a single jar from steamed rice and chili powder through a full year of sun on a rooftop in Sunchang, and ask what patience actually tastes like.

stories.title: Seoul After Midnight: A Street-Food Crawl
stories.excerpt: From tteokbokki carts under neon to charcoal grills in a Gwangjang alley, we eat our way across the city between 11pm and dawn—and find the dishes worth flying for hiding in plastic-stool corners.

stories.title: The Case for Funk: Learning to Love Doenjang
stories.excerpt: It smells like a dare and tastes like the ocean floor in the best way. A field guide to fermented soybean paste—how it's made, why it reads as savory, and the three dishes that will convert you for good.
